raw:
{
  "need": "Status",
  "secondary": { "name": "Identity" },
  "read": "When a newer hire is visibly stronger in a key area, the status dynamic runs both ways: they need to feel that their skill is genuinely seen and valued, not quietly managed or minimized so you look comfortable. If they sense you are downplaying it or keeping them in a lane that protects your ego, they will either show off to force the acknowledgment or disengage because mattering here feels impossible. The identity angle is that they are actively figuring out what kind of professional they are becoming, and your reaction to their competence is a major signal about whether this is a place that actually rewards being good.",
  "pull": { "collapse": "Enforcer", "instinct": "Lean on authority and seniority to keep them deferring to you on everything, including the area where they are sharper -- this backfires because they read it as insecurity, lose respect for you, and start looking for somewhere their skill will actually count." },
  "mentorMove": "Name what you see out loud and without flinching, then deliberately hand them real ownership in that area while making clear you are still the person responsible for their overall growth and the team's direction. That combination -- genuine acknowledgment plus a real stake -- is what turns their competence into commitment rather than restlessness.",
  "holdFirm": [
    "They still operate within team process, communicate decisions, and bring you in when something affects the broader group -- skill in one area does not mean operating as a solo agent.",
    "You hold the expectation that they keep developing in the areas where they are not yet strong, not just the one where they already shine."
  ],
  "stayFlexible": [
    "Let them lead, present, or own deliverables in the area where they are better -- do not water that down.",
    "Be open about what you are learning from them; modeling that learning goes both directions raises their status without you losing yours."
  ],
  "forceLevel": { "level": 2, "label": "Questions" },
  "script": [
    { "phase": "Connection", "words": "Hey, I want to have a straight conversation with you about something I have been sitting with. I think it is actually a good thing, but I want to say it directly instead of letting it stay unsaid." },
    { "phase": "Curiosity", "words": "You clearly have a stronger handle on this area than I do -- I think we both know it. What I am curious about is how you are experiencing that. Do you feel like you are actually getting to use it here, or does it feel like it is sitting on the shelf?" },
    { "phase": "Collaboration", "words": "Here is what I am thinking. I want to stop pretending the dynamic is something other than what it is. I would rather build something where you are genuinely running point on this, you are the person the team looks to, and I am the person helping you connect that skill to the bigger picture. What would make that feel real to you rather than just something I am saying?" },
    { "phase": "Commitment", "words": "I am going to hold you to the full job, not just the part you are already great at, because I think you are capable of being genuinely excellent across the board -- that is the standard I am working from. But on this specific area, I want you to own it. Let's agree on what that looks like so it is not vague." }
  ],
  "longGame": "The managers who keep strong young talent are the ones who never make them choose between their own growth and their loyalty to you -- make it obvious that their getting better makes the team better, and keep finding new edges for them to grow into so they are always a little stretched but never invisible."
}
situation: My newest hire is better at part of the job than I am and we both know it.
